description: Question bank based on Chapter 4.4 Social Issues for Karnataka FDA & SDA Examinations. Verify and expand questions before formal examination use.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What are social issues?

options.A: Personal problems affecting an individual only
options.B: Conditions or patterns affecting significant sections of society and requiring collective attention, public policy or social action
options.C: Issues related only to the economy
options.D: Problems that cannot be solved by society

questions.explanation: Social issues are conditions or patterns affecting significant sections of society and requiring collective attention, public policy or social action.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What makes an issue a social problem?

options.A: When it affects only one person
options.B: When it is ignored by society
options.C: When it is widely recognised as harmful, affects groups or institutions, and is considered to require collective or institutional action
options.D: When it is related only to the government

questions.explanation: A condition is treated as a social problem when it is widely recognised as harmful, affects groups or institutions, and is considered to require collective or institutional action.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is social policy?

options.A: Policies related to social media
options.B: Public measures and institutional arrangements intended to improve welfare, reduce deprivation and promote equality and social protection
options.C: Rules for social gatherings
options.D: Laws related to foreign policy

questions.explanation: Social policy refers to public measures and institutional arrangements intended to improve welfare, reduce deprivation and promote equality and social protection.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is social exclusion?

options.A: The process through which individuals or groups are prevented from participating fully in economic, social, cultural or political life
options.B: A process of including everyone in society
options.C: Exclusion from social media
options.D: A type of government policy

questions.explanation: Social exclusion is the process through which individuals or groups are prevented from participating fully in economic, social, cultural or political life.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is social inclusion?

options.A: Ensuring that all people can participate in society and access rights, services, opportunities and resources
options.B: Excluding certain groups from society
options.C: A type of social policy
options.D: A process of social exclusion

questions.explanation: Social inclusion aims to ensure that all people can participate in society and access rights, services, opportunities and resources.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is vulnerability?

options.A: Increased exposure to risks or harm combined with limited ability to prevent, withstand or recover from them
options.B: A state of being completely safe
options.C: A type of social policy
options.D: A process of social inclusion

questions.explanation: Vulnerability is increased exposure to risks or harm combined with limited ability to prevent, withstand or recover from them.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is intersectionality?

options.A: Examines how overlapping social identities and structures—such as caste, class, gender, disability and ethnicity—interact to shape different experiences of disadvantage or privilege
options.B: A type of social exclusion
options.C: A process of social inclusion
options.D: A government policy

questions.explanation: Intersectionality examines how overlapping social identities and structures—such as caste, class, gender, disability and ethnicity—interact to shape different experiences of disadvantage or privilege.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is affirmative action?

options.A: Targeted measures intended to address historical and structural disadvantage and improve access to education, employment or representation
options.B: A type of social exclusion
options.C: A process of social inclusion
options.D: A government policy related to foreign affairs

questions.explanation: Affirmative action refers to targeted measures intended to address historical and structural disadvantage and improve access to education, employment or representation.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is poverty?

options.A: A condition in which people lack adequate resources or capabilities to meet basic needs and maintain an acceptable standard of living
options.B: A condition of having excess resources
options.C: A type of social policy
options.D: A process of social inclusion

questions.explanation: Poverty is a condition in which people lack adequate resources or capabilities to meet basic needs and maintain an acceptable standard of living.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is absolute poverty?

options.A: Deprivation below a specified minimum standard of basic needs
options.B: Deprivation in relation to the income or living standards prevailing in a society
options.C: A type of social policy
options.D: A process of social inclusion

questions.explanation: Absolute poverty refers to deprivation below a specified minimum standard of basic needs.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is relative poverty?

options.A: Deprivation below a specified minimum standard of basic needs
options.B: Measures deprivation in relation to the income or living standards prevailing in a society
options.C: A type of social policy
options.D: A process of social inclusion

questions.explanation: Relative poverty measures deprivation in relation to the income or living standards prevailing in a society.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is multidimensional poverty?

options.A: Measures overlapping deprivations in areas such as health, education and living standards rather than income alone
options.B: Measures deprivation in relation to the income or living standards prevailing in a society
options.C: A type of social policy
options.D: A process of social inclusion

questions.explanation: Multidimensional poverty measures overlapping deprivations in areas such as health, education and living standards rather than income alone.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is a poverty line?

options.A: A threshold of income or consumption used to identify people whose resources fall below a defined minimum standard
options.B: A line drawn on a map to show poverty
options.C: A type of social policy
options.D: A process of social inclusion

questions.explanation: A poverty line is a threshold of income or consumption used to identify people whose resources fall below a defined minimum standard.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is the headcount ratio?

options.A: The proportion of the population living below the specified poverty line
options.B: The number of people living above the poverty line
options.C: A type of social policy
options.D: A process of social inclusion

questions.explanation: The headcount ratio is the proportion of the population living below the specified poverty line.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What does the poverty gap measure?

options.A: How far the income or consumption of poor people falls below the poverty line
options.B: The number of people living above the poverty line
options.C: A type of social policy
options.D: A process of social inclusion

questions.explanation: The poverty gap measures how far the income or consumption of poor people falls below the poverty line.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is the poverty gap index?

options.A: It measures the average shortfall from the poverty line across the whole population, counting non-poor people as having no shortfall
options.B: It measures the number of people living above the poverty line
options.C: A type of social policy
options.D: A process of social inclusion

questions.explanation: The poverty gap index measures the average shortfall from the poverty line across the whole population, counting non-poor people as having no shortfall.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is chronic poverty?

options.A: Poverty that persists over a long period or across generations
options.B: Temporary poverty caused by shocks
options.C: A type of social policy
options.D: A process of social inclusion

questions.explanation: Chronic poverty is poverty that persists over a long period or across generations.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is transient poverty?

options.A: Poverty that persists over a long period or across generations
options.B: Temporary poverty caused by shocks such as illness, job loss, crop failure or sudden economic disruption
options.C: A type of social policy
options.D: A process of social inclusion

questions.explanation: Transient poverty is temporary poverty caused by shocks such as illness, job loss, crop failure or sudden economic disruption.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is the vicious circle of poverty?

options.A: A self-reinforcing process in which low income leads to low saving and investment, low productivity and continued low income
options.B: A process of social inclusion
options.C: A type of social policy
options.D: A process of social exclusion

questions.explanation: The vicious circle of poverty is a self-reinforcing process in which low income leads to low saving and investment, low productivity and continued low income.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What are the major causes of poverty in India?

options.A: Unemployment and underemployment, low productivity, unequal access to land and assets, poor education and health, social discrimination, indebtedness, regional disparities and economic shocks
options.B: Only unemployment
options.C: Only low productivity
options.D: Only social discrimination

questions.explanation: Major causes include unemployment and underemployment, low productivity, unequal access to land and assets, poor education and health, social discrimination, indebtedness, regional disparities and economic shocks.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What are the major consequences of poverty?

options.A: Malnutrition, poor health, school dropout, child labour, insecure housing, indebtedness, social exclusion and reduced access to opportunities
options.B: Only malnutrition
options.C: Only poor health
options.D: Only child labour

questions.explanation: Consequences include malnutrition, poor health, school dropout, child labour, insecure housing, indebtedness, social exclusion and reduced access to opportunities.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is the difference between poverty and inequality?

options.A: Poverty concerns deprivation below a minimum standard; inequality concerns the distribution of income, wealth, opportunities or resources across society
options.B: Poverty concerns distribution; inequality concerns deprivation
options.C: Both are the same
options.D: Poverty is a type of inequality

questions.explanation: Poverty concerns deprivation below a minimum standard; inequality concerns the distribution of income, wealth, opportunities or resources across society.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is the Tendulkar Committee associated with?

options.A: It proposed a revised methodology for estimating poverty in India
options.B: It proposed an alternative methodology for estimating poverty in India
options.C: It proposed a new education policy
options.D: It proposed a new health policy

questions.explanation: The expert group chaired by Suresh D. Tendulkar proposed a revised methodology for estimating poverty in India.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is the Rangarajan Committee associated with?

options.A: It proposed a revised methodology for estimating poverty in India
options.B: It proposed an alternative methodology for estimating poverty in India
options.C: It proposed a new education policy
options.D: It proposed a new health policy

questions.explanation: The expert group chaired by C. Rangarajan proposed an alternative methodology for estimating poverty in India.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is the Global Multidimensional Poverty Index?

options.A: It is a measure of overlapping deprivations developed by the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative and the United Nations Development Programme
options.B: It is a measure of income poverty
options.C: It is a measure of relative poverty
options.D: It is a measure of absolute poverty

questions.explanation: The Global Multidimensional Poverty Index is a measure of overlapping deprivations developed by the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative and the United Nations Development Programme.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: Which three broad dimensions are commonly used in the global MPI?

options.A: Health, education and standard of living
options.B: Income, wealth and consumption
options.C: Food, clothing and shelter
options.D: Employment, education and health

questions.explanation: The three broad dimensions commonly used in the global MPI are health, education and standard of living.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is food security?

options.A: Food security exists when all people, at all times, have physical and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food for an active and healthy life
options.B: Food security exists when people have enough food for one day
options.C: Food security exists when people have access to food only during emergencies
options.D: Food security exists when people have access to food only in urban areas

questions.explanation: Food security exists when all people, at all times, have physical and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food for an active and healthy life.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is the National Food Security Act, 2013?

options.A: It provides a legal framework for subsidised foodgrains to eligible households and nutritional support to specified groups, subject to the Act and rules
options.B: It provides a legal framework for free education
options.C: It provides a legal framework for free healthcare
options.D: It provides a legal framework for free housing

questions.explanation: The National Food Security Act, 2013 provides a legal framework for subsidised foodgrains to eligible households and nutritional support to specified groups, subject to the Act and rules.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is the Public Distribution System (PDS)?

options.A: A government system for distributing essential commodities, especially subsidised foodgrains, to eligible beneficiaries through fair price shops
options.B: A system for distributing free education
options.C: A system for distributing free healthcare
options.D: A system for distributing free housing

questions.explanation: The PDS is a government system for distributing essential commodities, especially subsidised foodgrains, to eligible beneficiaries through fair price shops.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is Antyodaya Anna Yojana?

options.A: A food-security scheme launched in 2000 to provide highly subsidised foodgrains to the poorest eligible households
options.B: A scheme for free education
options.C: A scheme for free healthcare
options.D: A scheme for free housing

questions.explanation: Antyodaya Anna Yojana is a food-security scheme launched in 2000 to provide highly subsidised foodgrains to the poorest eligible households.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is MGNREGA?

options.A: The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005 provides a legal guarantee of up to 100 days of wage employment in a financial year to rural households whose adult members volunteer for unskilled manual work, subject to the Act
options.B: A scheme for free education
options.C: A scheme for free healthcare
options.D: A scheme for free housing

questions.explanation: MGNREGA is the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005. It provides a legal guarantee of up to 100 days of wage employment in a financial year to rural households whose adult members volunteer for unskilled manual work, subject to the Act.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is the National Rural Livelihoods Mission?

options.A: DAY-NRLM seeks to reduce rural poverty by promoting self-help groups, financial inclusion, livelihoods and community institutions
options.B: It seeks to reduce urban poverty
options.C: It seeks to improve education
options.D: It seeks to improve healthcare

questions.explanation: DAY-NRLM seeks to reduce rural poverty by promoting self-help groups, financial inclusion, livelihoods and community institutions.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is the National Urban Livelihoods Mission?

options.A: DAY-NULM aims to reduce urban poverty by supporting livelihoods, skill development, self-employment, shelters for the urban homeless and related interventions
options.B: It aims to reduce rural poverty
options.C: It aims to improve education
options.D: It aims to improve healthcare

questions.explanation: DAY-NULM aims to reduce urban poverty by supporting livelihoods, skill development, self-employment, shelters for the urban homeless and related interventions.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is direct benefit transfer (DBT)?

options.A: A mechanism for transferring eligible government benefits directly to beneficiaries' bank accounts, subject to scheme rules and verification
options.B: A mechanism for transferring benefits through intermediaries
options.C: A mechanism for transferring benefits in cash only
options.D: A mechanism for transferring benefits in kind only

questions.explanation: DBT is a mechanism for transferring eligible government benefits directly to beneficiaries' bank accounts, subject to scheme rules and verification.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is social security?

options.A: Public measures that protect people against risks such as old age, disability, sickness, unemployment and loss of income
options.B: Security provided by private companies
options.C: Security provided by individuals
options.D: Security provided by NGOs

questions.explanation: Social security consists of public measures that protect people against risks such as old age, disability, sickness, unemployment and loss of income.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is unemployment?

options.A: A condition in which a person who is in the labour force, available for work and seeking work does not have employment
options.B: A condition in which a person is not willing to work
options.C: A condition in which a person is retired
options.D: A condition in which a person is studying

questions.explanation: Unemployment is a condition in which a person who is in the labour force, available for work and seeking work does not have employment.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: Who is included in the labour force?

options.A: Employed persons and unemployed persons who meet the relevant availability and job-search criteria
options.B: Only employed persons
options.C: Only unemployed persons
options.D: All persons in the population

questions.explanation: The labour force includes employed persons and unemployed persons who meet the relevant availability and job-search criteria.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: How is the unemployment rate calculated?

options.A: Unemployed persons divided by the labour force, multiplied by 100
options.B: Unemployed persons divided by the total population, multiplied by 100
options.C: Employed persons divided by the labour force, multiplied by 100
options.D: Employed persons divided by the total population, multiplied by 100

questions.explanation: Unemployment rate = unemployed persons divided by the labour force, multiplied by 100.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is the labour force participation rate?

options.A: The proportion of the relevant population that is either employed or unemployed and actively participating in the labour force
options.B: The proportion of the relevant population that is employed
options.C: The proportion of the relevant population that is unemployed
options.D: The proportion of the relevant population that is not in the labour force

questions.explanation: Labour force participation rate is the proportion of the relevant population that is either employed or unemployed and actively participating in the labour force.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is the worker population ratio?

options.A: The proportion of the relevant population that is employed
options.B: The proportion of the relevant population that is unemployed
options.C: The proportion of the relevant population that is in the labour force
options.D: The proportion of the relevant population that is not in the labour force

questions.explanation: Worker population ratio is the proportion of the relevant population that is employed.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is open unemployment?

options.A: Occurs when a person willing and able to work cannot find a job
options.B: Occurs when more workers are engaged in an activity than are required
options.C: Occurs when work is available only during certain seasons
options.D: Occurs when people work fewer hours than they want

questions.explanation: Open unemployment occurs when a person willing and able to work cannot find a job.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is disguised unemployment?

options.A: Occurs when more workers are engaged in an activity than are required, so some can be withdrawn without reducing output
options.B: Occurs when a person willing and able to work cannot find a job
options.C: Occurs when work is available only during certain seasons
options.D: Occurs when people work fewer hours than they want

questions.explanation: Disguised unemployment occurs when more workers are engaged in an activity than are required, so some can be withdrawn without reducing output.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: Where is disguised unemployment commonly discussed in India?

options.A: In agriculture and family-based activities where surplus labour may be employed
options.B: In the IT sector
options.C: In the manufacturing sector
options.D: In the service sector

questions.explanation: Disguised unemployment is commonly discussed in agriculture and family-based activities where surplus labour may be employed.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is seasonal unemployment?

options.A: Occurs when work is available only during certain seasons or periods of the year
options.B: Occurs when a person willing and able to work cannot find a job
options.C: Occurs when more workers are engaged in an activity than are required
options.D: Occurs when people work fewer hours than they want

questions.explanation: Seasonal unemployment occurs when work is available only during certain seasons or periods of the year.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is educated unemployment?

options.A: Unemployment among people who possess formal education or qualifications but cannot obtain suitable work
options.B: Unemployment among people who have no education
options.C: Unemployment among people who are retired
options.D: Unemployment among people who are studying

questions.explanation: Educated unemployment refers to unemployment among people who possess formal education or qualifications but cannot obtain suitable work.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is structural unemployment?

options.A: Occurs when workers' skills, qualifications or locations do not match available jobs
options.B: Short-term unemployment arising when people move between jobs
options.C: Results from a downturn in economic activity
options.D: Occurs when technological change reduces demand for certain types of labour

questions.explanation: Structural unemployment occurs when workers' skills, qualifications or locations do not match available jobs.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is frictional unemployment?

options.A: Occurs when workers' skills, qualifications or locations do not match available jobs
options.B: Short-term unemployment arising when people move between jobs or enter the labour market
options.C: Results from a downturn in economic activity
options.D: Occurs when technological change reduces demand for certain types of labour

questions.explanation: Frictional unemployment is short-term unemployment arising when people move between jobs or enter the labour market.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is cyclical unemployment?

options.A: Occurs when workers' skills do not match jobs
options.B: Short-term unemployment when people move between jobs
options.C: Results from a downturn in economic activity and insufficient demand for labour
options.D: Occurs when technology reduces demand for labour

questions.explanation: Cyclical unemployment results from a downturn in economic activity and insufficient demand for labour.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is technological unemployment?

options.A: Occurs when workers' skills do not match jobs
options.B: Short-term unemployment when people move between jobs
options.C: Results from a downturn in economic activity
options.D: Occurs when technological change reduces demand for certain types of labour faster than workers can move into new jobs

questions.explanation: Technological unemployment occurs when technological change reduces demand for certain types of labour faster than workers can move into new jobs.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is underemployment?

options.A: Occurs when people work fewer hours than they want or perform work that does not adequately use their skills or productive capacity
options.B: Occurs when a person willing and able to work cannot find a job
options.C: Occurs when work is available only during certain seasons
options.D: Occurs when more workers are engaged in an activity than are required

questions.explanation: Underemployment occurs when people work fewer hours than they want or perform work that does not adequately use their skills or productive capacity.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is voluntary unemployment?

options.A: A situation in which a person chooses not to accept available employment at prevailing terms
options.B: A situation in which a person is willing to work but cannot obtain a job
options.C: A situation in which work is available only during certain seasons
options.D: A situation in which people work fewer hours than they want

questions.explanation: Voluntary unemployment refers to a situation in which a person chooses not to accept available employment at prevailing terms.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is involuntary unemployment?

options.A: A situation in which a person chooses not to accept available employment
options.B: Occurs when a person is willing to work at prevailing terms but cannot obtain a job
options.C: A situation in which work is available only during certain seasons
options.D: A situation in which people work fewer hours than they want

questions.explanation: Involuntary unemployment occurs when a person is willing to work at prevailing terms but cannot obtain a job.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What are the major causes of unemployment in India?

options.A: Skills mismatch, slow job creation in some sectors, seasonal agricultural work, population and labour-force growth, automation, regional imbalance and insufficient labour-intensive employment
options.B: Only skills mismatch
options.C: Only population growth
options.D: Only automation

questions.explanation: Major causes of unemployment in India include skills mismatch, slow job creation in some sectors, seasonal agricultural work, population and labour-force growth, automation, regional imbalance and insufficient labour-intensive employment.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS)?

options.A: A major Indian labour-force survey conducted by the National Statistical Office to provide estimates of employment, unemployment and labour-force participation
options.B: A survey conducted by the Reserve Bank of India
options.C: A survey conducted by the Ministry of Finance
options.D: A survey conducted by NITI Aayog

questions.explanation: PLFS is a major Indian labour-force survey conducted by the National Statistical Office to provide estimates of employment, unemployment and labour-force participation.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: Why must unemployment figures be read with their statistical definition?

options.A: Rates differ according to age group, survey period, usual status or current weekly status, and the definition of job search and availability
options.B: Because unemployment figures are always inaccurate
options.C: Because unemployment figures are not collected in India
options.D: Because unemployment figures are only collected in urban areas

questions.explanation: Unemployment figures must be read with their statistical definition because rates differ according to age group, survey period, usual status or current weekly status, and the definition of job search and availability.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is population?

options.A: The total number of people living in a defined geographical area at a specified time
options.B: The total number of people living in a country
options.C: The total number of people living in a state
options.D: The total number of people living in a city

questions.explanation: Population is the total number of people living in a defined geographical area at a specified time.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is demography?

options.A: The statistical and scientific study of human populations, including their size, composition, distribution and changes
options.B: The study of democracy
options.C: The study of human anatomy
options.D: The study of human behaviour

questions.explanation: Demography is the statistical and scientific study of human populations, including their size, composition, distribution and changes.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: Who is commonly regarded as a founder of modern demography?

options.A: John Graunt
options.B: Adam Smith
options.C: Thomas Malthus
options.D: Karl Marx

questions.explanation: John Graunt is often regarded as a pioneer of demographic statistics.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is population density?

options.A: The number of people living per unit of land area, commonly persons per square kilometre
options.B: The number of people living in a country
options.C: The number of people living in a city
options.D: The number of people living in a state

questions.explanation: Population density is the number of people living per unit of land area, commonly persons per square kilometre.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is the crude birth rate?

options.A: The number of live births per 1,000 people in a population during a year
options.B: The number of deaths per 1,000 people in a population during a year
options.C: The number of live births per 1,000 women in a population during a year
options.D: The number of deaths per 1,000 women in a population during a year

questions.explanation: Crude birth rate is the number of live births per 1,000 people in a population during a year.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is the crude death rate?

options.A: The number of live births per 1,000 people in a population during a year
options.B: The number of deaths per 1,000 people in a population during a year
options.C: The number of live births per 1,000 women in a population during a year
options.D: The number of deaths per 1,000 women in a population during a year

questions.explanation: Crude death rate is the number of deaths per 1,000 people in a population during a year.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is the infant mortality rate (IMR)?

options.A: The number of deaths of infants below one year of age per 1,000 live births during a specified period
options.B: The number of deaths of infants below five years of age per 1,000 live births
options.C: The number of deaths of mothers per 1,000 live births
options.D: The number of deaths of children below ten years of age per 1,000 live births

questions.explanation: IMR is the number of deaths of infants below one year of age per 1,000 live births during a specified period.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is the maternal mortality ratio (MMR)?

options.A: The number of maternal deaths per 100,000 live births during a specified period
options.B: The number of maternal deaths per 1,000 live births during a specified period
options.C: The number of maternal deaths per 10,000 live births during a specified period
options.D: The number of maternal deaths per 1,000 women during a specified period

questions.explanation: MMR is the number of maternal deaths per 100,000 live births during a specified period.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is the total fertility rate (TFR)?

options.A: The average number of children a woman would bear if she experienced the age-specific fertility rates of a given period throughout her reproductive years
options.B: The number of live births per 1,000 women in a population during a year
options.C: The number of live births per 1,000 people in a population during a year
options.D: The number of deaths per 1,000 people in a population during a year

questions.explanation: TFR is the average number of children a woman would bear if she experienced the age-specific fertility rates of a given period throughout her reproductive years.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is life expectancy at birth?

options.A: The average number of years a newborn would be expected to live if current age-specific mortality rates remained constant
options.B: The average number of years a person lives after retirement
options.C: The average number of years a person lives after marriage
options.D: The average number of years a person lives after birth

questions.explanation: Life expectancy at birth is the average number of years a newborn would be expected to live if current age-specific mortality rates remained constant.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is sex ratio in Indian census usage?

options.A: The number of females per 1,000 males
options.B: The number of males per 1,000 females
options.C: The number of females per 100 males
options.D: The number of males per 100 females

questions.explanation: In Indian census usage, sex ratio generally means the number of females per 1,000 males.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is child sex ratio in Indian Census reporting?

options.A: The number of girls per 1,000 boys in the 0-6 age group
options.B: The number of boys per 1,000 girls in the 0-6 age group
options.C: The number of girls per 1,000 boys in the 0-18 age group
options.D: The number of boys per 1,000 girls in the 0-18 age group

questions.explanation: Child sex ratio is the number of girls per 1,000 boys in the 0-6 age group in Indian Census reporting.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is age composition?

options.A: The distribution of a population across age groups
options.B: The distribution of a population across gender groups
options.C: The distribution of a population across income groups
options.D: The distribution of a population across geographical areas

questions.explanation: Age composition is the distribution of a population across age groups.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is dependency ratio?

options.A: Procedural justice concerns fairness, transparency and impartiality in the processes used to make decisions
options.B: Procedural justice concerns the fair allocation of resources
options.C: Procedural justice concerns respect for identity and dignity
options.D: Procedural justice concerns equality before the law

questions.explanation: Procedural justice concerns fairness, transparency and impartiality in the processes used to make decisions.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is recognition justice?

options.A: Recognition justice concerns respect for the identity, dignity, culture and equal status of individuals and groups
options.B: Recognition justice concerns the fair allocation of resources
options.C: Recognition justice concerns fairness in processes
options.D: Recognition justice concerns equality before the law

questions.explanation: Recognition justice concerns respect for the identity, dignity, culture and equal status of individuals and groups.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is substantive equality?

options.A: Substantive equality recognises that equal treatment alone may not remove structural barriers and supports measures that enable genuinely equal participation and outcomes
options.B: Substantive equality means equal treatment only
options.C: Substantive equality means formal equality only
options.D: Substantive equality means equality before the law only

questions.explanation: Substantive equality recognises that equal treatment alone may not remove structural barriers and supports measures that enable genuinely equal participation and outcomes.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is constitutional morality?

options.A: Constitutional morality means respect for constitutional values, procedures, rights and institutional limits in public and civic life
options.B: Constitutional morality means respect for personal morality only
options.C: Constitutional morality means respect for religious morality only
options.D: Constitutional morality means respect for social morality only

questions.explanation: Constitutional morality means respect for constitutional values, procedures, rights and institutional limits in public and civic life.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: Which words in the Preamble express the Constitution's social objectives?

options.A: Justice—social, economic and political; liberty; equality; and fraternity
options.B: Justice—social only
options.C: Liberty and equality only
options.D: Fraternity only

questions.explanation: The words in the Preamble that express the Constitution's social objectives are Justice—social, economic and political; liberty; equality; and fraternity.

options.D: Article 17

options.B: Article 14

options.D: Article 17

questions.question: Which article abolishes titles, subject to constitutional exceptions?

options.B: Article 17

options.D: Article 15

questions.explanation: Article 18 abolishes titles, subject to constitutional exceptions.

questions.question: Which article prohibits trafficking in human beings and forced labour?

options.B: Article 24

options.D: Article 17

questions.question: Which article prohibits child employment in factories, mines and other hazardous employment specified by the provision?

options.A: Article 24
options.B: Article 23
options.C: Article 21A
options.D: Article 17

questions.explanation: Article 24 prohibits child employment in factories, mines and other hazardous employment specified by the provision.

options.D: Article 42

options.D: Article 39(d)

questions.question: Which Directive Principle addresses adequate means of livelihood and distribution of material resources?

options.C: Article 46
options.D: Article 42

questions.explanation: Article 39, including clauses (a) and (b), addresses adequate means of livelihood and distribution of material resources.

questions.question: Which Directive Principle concerns equal pay for equal work for men and women?

options.D: Article 39(c)

questions.question: Which Directive Principle concerns protection of workers' health and strength and children's development?

options.C: Article 41 and Article 42
options.D: Article 45 and Article 46

questions.explanation: Article 39(e) and Article 39(f) concern protection of workers' health and strength and children's development.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: Which article directs the State to promote educational and economic interests of weaker sections, particularly SCs and STs?

options.A: Article 46
options.B: Article 38
options.C: Article 39
options.D: Article 42

questions.explanation: Article 46 directs the State to promote educational and economic interests of weaker sections, particularly SCs and STs.

questions.question: Which article provides for a National Commission for Scheduled Castes?

options.A: Article 338
options.B: Article 338A

options.D: Article 341

questions.question: Which article provides for a National Commission for Scheduled Tribes?

questions.question: Which article provides for a National Commission for Backward Classes?

options.A: Article 338B
options.B: Article 338

options.D: Article 342A

questions.question: What is the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955?

options.C: It provides penalties for manual scavenging

questions.explanation: The Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 provides penalties for the practice of untouchability and enforcement of rights arising from its abolition.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989?

options.A: It prevents atrocities against members of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes and provides for special courts, relief and rehabilitation measures
options.B: It prevents untouchability
options.C: It prevents manual scavenging
options.D: It prevents dowry

questions.explanation: The SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 prevents atrocities against members of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes and provides for special courts, relief and rehabilitation measures.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is affirmative action in India?

options.A: It includes constitutionally and legally authorised measures such as reservation and targeted support to address historical disadvantage and improve representation
options.B: It includes only reservation measures
options.C: It includes only targeted support measures
options.D: It includes only constitutional measures

questions.explanation: Affirmative action in India includes constitutionally and legally authorised measures such as reservation and targeted support to address historical disadvantage and improve representation.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is the role of the National Human Rights Commission?

options.A: The NHRC is a statutory body under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 that protects and promotes human rights through inquiries, recommendations and related functions
options.B: The NHRC is a constitutional body under Article 338
options.C: The NHRC is a statutory body under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 2000
options.D: The NHRC is a constitutional body under Article 338A

questions.explanation: The NHRC is a statutory body under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 that protects and promotes human rights through inquiries, recommendations and related functions.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is the role of the State Human Rights Commission?

options.A: It performs human-rights functions within the jurisdiction and framework provided by the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993
options.B: It performs human-rights functions only at the national level
options.C: It performs human-rights functions only at the district level
options.D: It performs human-rights functions only at the village level

questions.explanation: The State Human Rights Commission performs human-rights functions within the jurisdiction and framework provided by the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is legal aid?

options.A: Legal aid provides legal services to eligible persons who cannot afford them, helping ensure access to justice
options.B: Legal aid provides legal services to all persons free of cost
options.C: Legal aid provides legal services only to women
options.D: Legal aid provides legal services only to children

questions.explanation: Legal aid provides legal services to eligible persons who cannot afford them, helping ensure access to justice.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: Which constitutional article directs the State to provide free legal aid?

options.A: Article 39A
options.B: Article 39(d)
options.C: Article 38
options.D: Article 46

questions.explanation: Article 39A directs the State to provide free legal aid.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is the National Legal Services Authority (NALSA)?

options.A: NALSA is a statutory authority constituted under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 to provide free legal services to eligible persons and organise Lok Adalats
options.B: NALSA is a constitutional authority under Article 39A
options.C: NALSA is a statutory authority under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 2000
options.D: NALSA is a statutory authority under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993

questions.explanation: NALSA is a statutory authority constituted under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 to provide free legal services to eligible persons and organise Lok Adalats.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is a Lok Adalat?

options.A: A Lok Adalat is an alternative dispute-resolution forum established under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 to facilitate settlement of specified disputes
options.B: A Lok Adalat is a regular court
options.C: A Lok Adalat is a tribunal under the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007
options.D: A Lok Adalat is a commission under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993

questions.explanation: A Lok Adalat is an alternative dispute-resolution forum established under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 to facilitate settlement of specified disputes.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is migration?

options.A: The movement of people from one place to another, involving a change of usual residence or crossing a defined boundary for a specified period
options.B: The movement of goods from one place to another
options.C: The movement of animals from one place to another
options.D: The movement of capital from one place to another

questions.explanation: Migration is the movement of people from one place to another, involving a change of usual residence or crossing a defined boundary for a specified period.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is internal migration?

options.A: Movement within the boundaries of the same country
options.B: Movement across national borders
options.C: Movement from rural to urban areas
options.D: Movement from urban to rural areas

questions.explanation: Internal migration is movement within the boundaries of the same country.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is international migration?

options.A: Movement across national borders
options.B: Movement within the boundaries of the same country
options.C: Movement from rural to urban areas
options.D: Movement from urban to rural areas

questions.explanation: International migration is movement across national borders.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is rural-to-urban migration?

options.A: Movement from rural areas to towns or cities
options.B: Movement from towns or cities to rural areas
options.C: Movement within rural areas
options.D: Movement within urban areas

questions.explanation: Rural-to-urban migration is movement from rural areas to towns or cities.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is urban-to-rural migration?

options.A: Movement from towns or cities to rural areas
options.B: Movement from rural areas to towns or cities
options.C: Movement within rural areas
options.D: Movement within urban areas

questions.explanation: Urban-to-rural migration is movement from towns or cities to rural areas.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is seasonal migration?

options.A: Temporary movement linked to recurring work or seasonal conditions, such as agricultural cycles
options.B: Permanent movement from one place to another
options.C: Movement across national borders
options.D: Movement within the same city

questions.explanation: Seasonal migration is temporary movement linked to recurring work or seasonal conditions, such as agricultural cycles.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is circular migration?

options.A: Repeated movement between an origin and destination, often for work, without permanent settlement at the destination
options.B: One-time movement from origin to destination
options.C: Movement across national borders
options.D: Movement within the same city

questions.explanation: Circular migration is repeated movement between an origin and destination, often for work, without permanent settlement at the destination.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is forced migration?

options.A: Occurs when people are compelled to leave their homes because of conflict, persecution, disasters, development projects or other serious threats
options.B: Occurs when people move primarily by choice
options.C: Occurs when people move for education
options.D: Occurs when people move for family reasons

questions.explanation: Forced migration occurs when people are compelled to leave their homes because of conflict, persecution, disasters, development projects or other serious threats.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is voluntary migration?

options.A: Occurs when people move primarily by choice, often for work, education, family or quality-of-life reasons
options.B: Occurs when people are compelled to leave their homes
options.C: Occurs when people move due to conflict
options.D: Occurs when people move due to disasters

questions.explanation: Voluntary migration occurs when people move primarily by choice, often for work, education, family or quality-of-life reasons.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What are push factors of migration?

options.A: Conditions that encourage people to leave, such as unemployment, poverty, conflict, environmental stress, discrimination or lack of services
options.B: Conditions that attract people to a destination
options.C: Conditions that encourage people to stay
options.D: Conditions that have no effect on migration

questions.explanation: Push factors of migration are conditions that encourage people to leave, such as unemployment, poverty, conflict, environmental stress, discrimination or lack of services.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What are pull factors of migration?

options.A: Conditions that attract people to a destination, such as jobs, education, healthcare, higher wages and better infrastructure
options.B: Conditions that encourage people to leave
options.C: Conditions that encourage people to stay
options.D: Conditions that have no effect on migration

questions.explanation: Pull factors of migration are conditions that attract people to a destination, such as jobs, education, healthcare, higher wages and better infrastructure.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is a migrant worker?

options.A: A person who moves from their usual place of residence to another place for employment
options.B: A person who moves from their usual place of residence to another place for education
options.C: A person who moves from their usual place of residence to another place for family reasons
options.D: A person who moves from their usual place of residence to another place for tourism

questions.explanation: A migrant worker is a person who moves from their usual place of residence to another place for employment.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is remittance?

options.A: Money sent by a migrant to family members or others, commonly in the place of origin
options.B: Money sent by a family member to a migrant
options.C: Money sent by the government to migrants
options.D: Money sent by employers to migrants

questions.explanation: A remittance is money sent by a migrant to family members or others, commonly in the place of origin.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What are the positive effects of migration?

options.A: Migration can improve income, employment, skills, education, household resilience and the flow of remittances
options.B: Migration can only improve income
options.C: Migration can only improve employment
options.D: Migration can only improve skills

questions.explanation: Positive effects of migration include improvement in income, employment, skills, education, household resilience and the flow of remittances.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What are the negative effects or challenges associated with migration?

options.A: Migrants may face insecure work, poor housing, discrimination, limited access to welfare, family separation, exploitation and language barriers
options.B: Migrants may face only insecure work
options.C: Migrants may face only poor housing
options.D: Migrants may face only discrimination

questions.explanation: Negative effects or challenges associated with migration include insecure work, poor housing, discrimination, limited access to welfare, family separation, exploitation and language barriers.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is brain drain?

options.A: The movement of highly educated or skilled people from one region or country to another, potentially reducing the supply of skills in the place of origin
options.B: The movement of unskilled people from one region or country to another
options.C: The movement of capital from one region or country to another
options.D: The movement of goods from one region or country to another

questions.explanation: Brain drain is the movement of highly educated or skilled people from one region or country to another, potentially reducing the supply of skills in the place of origin.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is brain gain?

options.A: An increase in skilled human resources through inward migration, return migration or knowledge transfer
options.B: A decrease in skilled human resources through outward migration
options.C: The movement of unskilled people from one region to another
options.D: The movement of capital from one region to another

questions.explanation: Brain gain is an increase in skilled human resources through inward migration, return migration or knowledge transfer.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is the difference between a refugee and an internally displaced person?

options.A: A refugee crosses an international border and meets the relevant refugee definition; an internally displaced person is forced to flee home but remains within their own country
options.B: A refugee remains within their own country; an internally displaced person crosses an international border
options.C: Both cross international borders
options.D: Both remain within their own country

questions.explanation: A refugee crosses an international border and meets the relevant refugee definition; an internally displaced person is forced to flee home but remains within their own country.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is migrant portability of welfare?

options.A: Portability allows eligible migrants to access specified benefits across locations, subject to scheme rules and implementation
options.B: Portability allows eligible migrants to access benefits only in their place of origin
options.C: Portability allows eligible migrants to access benefits only in their destination
options.D: Portability allows eligible migrants to access benefits only at the national level

questions.explanation: Migrant portability of welfare allows eligible migrants to access specified benefits across locations, subject to scheme rules and implementation.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is One Nation One Ration Card?

options.B: It is a portability initiative for education
options.C: It is a portability initiative for healthcare
options.D: It is a portability initiative for employment

questions.explanation: One Nation One Ration Card is a portability initiative that enables eligible National Food Security Act ration-card beneficiaries to obtain entitled foodgrains from fair price shops across participating States and Union Territories.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is urbanisation?

options.A: The process through which an increasing proportion of the population lives in urban areas, accompanied by the growth and expansion of towns and cities
options.B: The process through which an increasing proportion of the population lives in rural areas
options.C: The process of decreasing population in urban areas
options.D: The process of decreasing population in rural areas

questions.explanation: Urbanisation is the process through which an increasing proportion of the population lives in urban areas, accompanied by the growth and expansion of towns and cities.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is urban growth?

options.A: An increase in the population or physical size of an urban settlement
options.B: A decrease in the population or physical size of an urban settlement
options.C: An increase in the population or physical size of a rural settlement
options.D: A decrease in the population or physical size of a rural settlement

questions.explanation: Urban growth is an increase in the population or physical size of an urban settlement.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is the difference between urbanisation and urban growth?

options.A: Urbanisation refers especially to an increase in the urban share of population; urban growth refers to an increase in the size or number of urban residents
options.B: Urbanisation refers to an increase in the size of urban settlements; urban growth refers to an increase in the urban share of population
options.C: Both are the same
options.D: Urbanisation refers to rural growth; urban growth refers to urban decline

questions.explanation: Urbanisation refers especially to an increase in the urban share of population; urban growth refers to an increase in the size or number of urban residents.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What are the major causes of urbanisation?

options.A: Industrialisation, employment, migration, education, services, transport, administrative expansion and natural increase in urban populations
options.B: Only industrialisation
options.C: Only employment
options.D: Only migration

questions.explanation: Major causes of urbanisation include industrialisation, employment, migration, education, services, transport, administrative expansion and natural increase in urban populations.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is a megacity?

options.A: An urban agglomeration with a population of 10 million or more under the commonly used UN definition
options.B: An urban agglomeration with a population of 1 million or more
options.C: An urban agglomeration with a population of 5 million or more
options.D: An urban agglomeration with a population of 20 million or more

questions.explanation: A megacity is an urban agglomeration with a population of 10 million or more under the commonly used UN definition.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is an urban agglomeration in Indian Census usage?

options.A: It is a continuous urban spread consisting of a town and adjoining outgrowths, or two or more physically contiguous towns with or without outgrowths, meeting Census criteria
options.B: It is a rural settlement
options.C: It is a single town without outgrowths
options.D: It is a group of villages

questions.explanation: An urban agglomeration in Indian Census usage is a continuous urban spread consisting of a town and adjoining outgrowths, or two or more physically contiguous towns with or without outgrowths, meeting Census criteria.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is a slum?

options.A: A densely populated urban settlement or area characterised by inadequate housing and one or more forms of deprivation, such as insecure tenure, poor sanitation or inadequate services
options.B: A densely populated rural settlement
options.C: A sparsely populated urban settlement
options.D: A sparsely populated rural settlement

questions.explanation: A slum is a densely populated urban settlement or area characterised by inadequate housing and one or more forms of deprivation, such as insecure tenure, poor sanitation or inadequate services.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is suburbanisation?

options.A: The expansion of population and activities from a central city into surrounding suburban areas
options.B: The expansion of population and activities from suburban areas into the central city
options.C: The expansion of population and activities from rural areas into urban areas
options.D: The expansion of population and activities from urban areas into rural areas

questions.explanation: Suburbanisation is the expansion of population and activities from a central city into surrounding suburban areas.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is counter-urbanisation?

options.A: Movement of people or activities from large urban centres to smaller towns or rural areas
options.B: Movement of people or activities from smaller towns to large urban centres
options.C: Movement of people or activities from rural areas to urban areas
options.D: Movement of people or activities within the same urban area

questions.explanation: Counter-urbanisation is movement of people or activities from large urban centres to smaller towns or rural areas.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is urban sprawl?

options.A: The outward expansion of low-density or poorly coordinated urban development into surrounding areas
options.B: The inward expansion of high-density urban development
options.C: The expansion of rural development into urban areas
options.D: The contraction of urban development

questions.explanation: Urban sprawl is the outward expansion of low-density or poorly coordinated urban development into surrounding areas.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is gentrification?

options.A: A process in which investment and higher-income residents move into a lower-income urban area, often increasing property values and potentially displacing existing residents
options.B: A process in which investment and lower-income residents move into a higher-income urban area
options.C: A process in which rural residents move into urban areas
options.D: A process in which urban residents move into rural areas

questions.explanation: Gentrification is a process in which investment and higher-income residents move into a lower-income urban area, often increasing property values and potentially displacing existing residents.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What are common problems caused by rapid urbanisation?

options.A: Housing shortages, slums, congestion, pollution, inadequate water and sanitation, waste-management challenges, pressure on transport and infrastructure, and urban inequality
options.B: Only housing shortages
options.C: Only congestion
options.D: Only pollution

questions.explanation: Common problems caused by rapid urbanisation include housing shortages, slums, congestion, pollution, inadequate water and sanitation, waste-management challenges, pressure on transport and infrastructure, and urban inequality.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What are positive effects of urbanisation?

options.A: Urbanisation can increase access to employment, education, healthcare, markets, innovation, infrastructure and cultural exchange
options.B: Urbanisation can only increase access to employment
options.C: Urbanisation can only increase access to education
options.D: Urbanisation can only increase access to healthcare

questions.explanation: Positive effects of urbanisation include increased access to employment, education, healthcare, markets, innovation, infrastructure and cultural exchange.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is urban poverty?

options.A: Deprivation among people living in towns and cities, often involving insecure work, high housing costs, poor services and vulnerability
options.B: Deprivation among people living in villages
options.C: Deprivation among people living in forests
options.D: Deprivation among people living in hills

questions.explanation: Urban poverty is deprivation among people living in towns and cities, often involving insecure work, high housing costs, poor services and vulnerability.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is urban planning?

options.A: The organised management of land use, housing, transport, infrastructure, public spaces and services to guide urban development
options.B: The organised management of agricultural land
options.C: The organised management of forests
options.D: The organised management of mines

questions.explanation: Urban planning is the organised management of land use, housing, transport, infrastructure, public spaces and services to guide urban development.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is sustainable urbanisation?

options.A: Sustainable urbanisation seeks to make cities inclusive, safe, resilient and environmentally sustainable
options.B: Sustainable urbanisation seeks to make cities exclusive and unsafe
options.C: Sustainable urbanisation seeks to make villages inclusive and safe
options.D: Sustainable urbanisation seeks to make forests inclusive and safe

questions.explanation: Sustainable urbanisation seeks to make cities inclusive, safe, resilient and environmentally sustainable.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is the Smart Cities Mission?

options.B: The Smart Cities Mission was launched in 2010
options.C: The Smart Cities Mission was launched in 2020
options.D: The Smart Cities Mission was launched in 2005

questions.explanation: The Smart Cities Mission was launched in 2015 to promote sustainable and inclusive cities through area-based development and smart solutions; consult current official programme information for its present status.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is the Swachh Bharat Mission-Urban?

options.A: It is a national programme focused on urban sanitation, solid waste management and cleanliness
options.B: It is a national programme focused on rural sanitation
options.C: It is a national programme focused on urban education
options.D: It is a national programme focused on urban health

questions.explanation: Swachh Bharat Mission-Urban is a national programme focused on urban sanitation, solid waste management and cleanliness.

questions.question: What is the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana-Urban?

options.A: PMAY-U is a housing programme intended to support eligible urban households in accessing affordable housing, subject to current scheme guidelines and phases
options.B: PMAY-U is a housing programme for rural households
options.C: PMAY-U is an education programme for urban households
options.D: PMAY-U is a health programme for urban households

questions.explanation: PMAY-U is a housing programme intended to support eligible urban households in accessing affordable housing, subject to current scheme guidelines and phases.

questions.subject: Social Issues
questions.question: What is the 74th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992?

options.A: It gave constitutional recognition to urban local bodies and inserted Part IX-A and the Twelfth Schedule
options.B: It gave constitutional recognition to rural local bodies and inserted Part IX and the Eleventh Schedule
options.C: It gave constitutional recognition to cooperative societies
options.D: It gave constitutional recognition to the National Commission for Backward Classes

questions.explanation: The 74th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992 gave constitutional recognition to urban local bodies and inserted Part IX-A and the Twelfth Schedule.
